Stage 2 · Sensor faults · Simulated test world: 579 wells, two datasets

The pump is a second depth gauge.

A pump that lifts water from deeper needs more power for the same flow. So every pumping session carries a depth measurement that does not depend on the level sensor at all. When the two disagree for weeks, the level sensor is the one that has gone wrong.

Faulty level sensors found, dataset A88 %52 of 59; dataset B: 80 % (43 of 54)
Healthy wells wrongly flagged6 of 520dataset B: 10 of 525
Sudden offsets: found / typical delay95 % · 5 wkdataset B: 84 % · 5 weeks
Error on faulty-sensor wells, now1.11 m2.68 m without this layer; 3.01 m for the gauge

How the check works

Depth from the pump

x = (P − Pstandby) ÷ Q  ≈  α + κ · depth

power drawn above standby, per unit of flow, grows in a straight line with the depth the water is lifted from

For each well, α and κ are fitted from its first readings: κ across the training years, α over the first 30 days, when the sensor is taken to be freshly installed and correct. Each start-of-session reading is then compared with the depth the pump implies.

residual = reading − (x − α) ÷ κ

a healthy sensor's weekly residual wanders around zero; a faulty one walks away

From residual to correction

  1. Take the median residual of each week.
  2. Compare the median of the last four weeks with the well's own week-to-week scatter.
  3. If it sits outside 0.6 m and four standard errors for three weeks in a row, start correcting the readings by that amount. Stop when it falls back below half the threshold.
  4. Separately: drop readings that are impossible (below ground level or deeper than 300 m), far from the last 15 readings, or frozen (a stop reading identical to the start reading).

Every step uses only earlier weeks, so a forecast never benefits from knowing what comes after it.

One well of each kind, chosen as a typical case: caught after the fault began, with no false correction before it. Grey dots: the weekly residual. Blue line: the correction the model applied.

Detection, fault by fault

A well counts as flagged after four corrected weeks or three frozen sessions. Delay is from the fault's start to the first flag.

Slow drifts are the hard case: for months they look like a real change in the water table. A drift of 0.5 m a year takes over a year to clear the threshold.

What building it taught us

Use the first five-minute record, not the last

The pump's last record comes one five-minute step before the stop reading. In short sessions where the water falls fast, the level drops up to about 1 m in that step, enough to bend the calibration by 5–12 %. The first record and the start reading describe the same moment.

Calibrate across years, not weeks

Over a few weeks the start readings barely move, and the sensor's own noise then flattens the fitted line by up to 10 %. In the first version that looked like drift in over a hundred wells. Fitting across the training years, with fault-affected months set aside, removed it.

Ask for three weeks in a row

A single odd week is usually noise, and low-flow wells are noisier than most. Scaling the threshold to each well's own scatter and requiring three weeks in a row, together with the two fixes before it, cut the wells flagged from 263 to 58, close to the 59 that really had faulty sensors.

How far this will carry to the field

In the simulator the meters are clean (power ±2 %, flow ±3 %) and nothing changes the pump's efficiency: no pipe friction, no wear, no replaced pump. Real pumps will be noisier, and a pump replacement will look like a sensor fault until it is recorded. The vendor's real exports already carry power and flow every five minutes, so this check can be tried on real wells as soon as matching real levels are available.

Borewell Forecast is a proof of concept for forecasting groundwater levels in Bengaluru borewells. Results are labelled by where the data came from: vendor export (15 days, July 2026, in the vendor's real format but with demonstration water-level values), synthetic test system (450 simulated wells with a known answer) or digital twin (a physics-based simulation of the 579 wells over a year). No real water-level measurement has been used yet, and nothing here is yet a validated field forecast.
